# Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function of a Finite Real Spectrum

For a finite family of real numbers `s : Fin n → ℝ` (a "spectrum"), the empirical
cumulative distribution function (CDF) at a point `x` is the fraction of indices `i`
with `s i ≤ x`.

This file defines `empiricalCDF` together with an affine renormalization
`renormSpectrum`, and proves a collection of elementary properties: nonnegativity,
the upper bound `1`, membership in `[0,1]`, monotonicity in `x`, invariance under
permutations of the indices, stability under uniform perturbations of the spectrum,
and the behaviour under a positive affine renormalization.
-/

import Mathlib

open Finset

open scoped BigOperators

namespace EmpiricalSpectrumCDF

/-- The empirical cumulative distribution function of a finite real spectrum
`s : Fin n → ℝ`: the fraction of indices `i` with `s i ≤ x`. -/
noncomputable def empiricalCDF {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ((Finset.univ.filter (fun i => s i ≤ x)).card : ℝ) / (n : ℝ)

/-- Affine renormalization of a spectrum: `i ↦ a * s i + b`. -/
def renormSpectrum {n : ℕ} (a b : ℝ) (s : Fin n → ℝ) : Fin n → ℝ :=
  fun i => a * s i + b

/-- The empirical CDF is nonnegative. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_nonneg {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    0 ≤ empiricalCDF s x := by
  exact div_nonneg ( Nat.cast_nonneg _ ) ( Nat.cast_nonneg _ )

/-- The empirical CDF is at most `1`. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_le_one {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    empiricalCDF s x ≤ 1 := by
  exact div_le_one_of_le₀ ( mod_cast le_trans ( Finset.card_filter_le _ _ ) ( by norm_num ) ) ( Nat.cast_nonneg _ )

/-- The empirical CDF lies in `[0, 1]`. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_mem_Icc {n : ℕ} [NeZero n] (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ) :
    empiricalCDF s x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1 := by
  exact ⟨ empiricalCDF_nonneg s x, empiricalCDF_le_one s x ⟩

/-- The empirical CDF is monotone in `x`. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_mono {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → ℝ) {x y : ℝ} (hxy : x ≤ y) :
    empiricalCDF s x ≤ empiricalCDF s y := by
  exact div_le_div_of_nonneg_right ( mod_cast Finset.card_mono <| fun i hi => Finset.mem_filter.mpr ⟨ Finset.mem_univ i, le_trans ( Finset.mem_filter.mp hi |>.2 ) hxy ⟩ ) ( Nat.cast_nonneg _ )

/-- The empirical CDF is invariant under permutations of the indices. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_perm {n : ℕ} (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ) (π : Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) :
    empiricalCDF (s ∘ π) x = empiricalCDF s x := by
  unfold empiricalCDF
  rw [Finset.card_filter, Finset.card_filter]
  simp only [Function.comp_apply]
  rw [Equiv.sum_comp π fun i => if s i ≤ x then 1 else 0]

/-- If `s` and `t` are uniformly `ε`-close, the CDF of `s` at `x - ε` is at most the
CDF of `t` at `x`. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_perturb_le {n : ℕ} (s t : Fin n → ℝ) (x ε : ℝ)
    (h : ∀ i, |s i - t i| ≤ ε) :
    empiricalCDF s (x - ε) ≤ empiricalCDF t x := by
  refine div_le_div_of_nonneg_right (mod_cast ?_) (Nat.cast_nonneg _)
  exact Finset.card_mono fun i hi => by norm_num at *; linarith [abs_le.mp (h i)]

/-- The symmetric perturbation inequality, swapping `s` and `t`. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_perturb_le_symm {n : ℕ} (s t : Fin n → ℝ) (x ε : ℝ)
    (h : ∀ i, |s i - t i| ≤ ε) :
    empiricalCDF t (x - ε) ≤ empiricalCDF s x :=
  empiricalCDF_perturb_le t s x ε (fun i => by rw [abs_sub_comm]; exact h i)

/-- The empirical CDF of a positively renormalized spectrum. -/
theorem empiricalCDF_renorm_pos {n : ℕ} (a b : ℝ) (s : Fin n → ℝ) (x : ℝ)
    (ha : 0 < a) :
    empiricalCDF (renormSpectrum a b s) x = empiricalCDF s ((x - b) / a) := by
  unfold empiricalCDF renormSpectrum
  simp only [add_comm, le_div_iff₀' ha, le_sub_iff_add_le]

end EmpiricalSpectrumCDF

# Future Directions

Building on the deterministic empirical spectral CDF substrate in
`MachineLearning/EmpiricalSpectrumCDF.lean`, we outline original directions for
extending the theory. Each is deliberately scoped to remain a deterministic or
classical-analysis contribution, providing verified scaffolding for later
probabilistic spectral-universality work without overclaiming about trained
models.

## 1. From finite spectra to matrix singular values

This direction lifts the empirical CDF from an abstract function `Fin n → ℝ` to
the genuine spectrum of a matrix, defining `singularSpectrum : Matrix (Fin m)
(Fin n) ℝ → Fin (min m n) → ℝ` via Mathlib's singular-value / eigenvalue API and
specializing every theorem in the substrate to it. One would prove that the
empirical singular-value CDF inherits range, monotonicity, permutation invariance
(now automatic, since singular values are intrinsically unordered), the
Kolmogorov shift bound under matrix perturbations, and renormalization
compatibility under scalar scaling of the matrix. The key insight is that
Weyl-type singular-value perturbation inequalities convert an *operator-norm*
bound `‖A - B‖ ≤ ε` into exactly the *coordinatewise* spectral bound
`|σ_i(A) - σ_i(B)| ≤ ε` that our `empiricalCDF_perturb_le` already consumes, so
the entire stability theory transfers with no new probabilistic input. Why now?
Mathlib already carries enough linear-algebra spectral theory (eigenvalues of
symmetric maps, the spectral theorem) that the bridge from finite spectra to real
matrices is buildable today, and it is the single highest-leverage step toward
talking about actual weight-matrix spectra.

## 2. Wasserstein- and Kolmogorov-style metrics on spectra

Here one formalizes quantitative distances between empirical spectral measures:
the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance `sup_x |empiricalCDF s x - empiricalCDF t x|` and
the 1-Wasserstein distance between the associated empirical measures, then proves
the deterministic perturbation bounds `KS(s, t) ≤ (controlled by ε)` and
`W₁(s, t) ≤ (1/n) Σ_i |s_{(i)} - t_{(i)}|` for sorted spectra. The key insight is
that our two directional shift lemmas, `empiricalCDF_perturb_le` and
`empiricalCDF_perturb_le'`, are already the two halves of a sandwich that pins the
KS distance, so the metric-level statements are corollaries of inequalities we
have proved rather than fresh theorems. Why now? With the directional shift bounds
in hand, the remaining work is the order-statistics rearrangement argument
(Mathlib's `MonovaryOn`/rearrangement and `Tuple.sort` machinery), which is
self-contained and avoids any measure-theoretic limit, making this a clean
near-term extension.

## 3. Histogram and binning statistics with refinement consistency

This direction introduces a histogram functor that buckets a spectrum into a
finite family of bins `[c_k, c_{k+1})` and expresses each bin mass as a telescoping
difference `empiricalCDF s c_{k+1} - empiricalCDF s c_k`, proving that bin masses
are nonnegative, sum to one, and behave monotonically under bin refinement. The
key insight is that every histogram quantity is a *finite difference* of the
empirical CDF, so monotonicity (`empiricalCDF_mono`) and the range bounds
immediately certify that histograms are bona fide probability vectors and that
refining a partition only redistributes mass within parent bins. Why now? Spectral
histograms are the format in which empirical universality is actually *visualized*
and reported in the LLM literature, so providing a verified, refinement-consistent
histogram layer directly connects the formal substrate to how practitioners
measure spectra, and it needs nothing beyond the lemmas already proved.

## 4. Quantiles, spectral gaps, and spacing distributions

Here one defines the empirical quantile function as a generalized inverse
`quantile s p = inf { x | p ≤ empiricalCDF s x }`, establishes the
Galois-style duality `empiricalCDF s x ≥ p ↔ quantile s p ≤ x`, and from it builds
spectral gaps (consecutive-quantile differences) and the empirical spacing
distribution that random-matrix universality (e.g. Wigner surmise) is ultimately
about. The key insight is that monotonicity and the `[0,1]` range of the empirical
CDF make it precisely a monotone, bounded function whose generalized inverse is
well behaved, so the quantile/CDF adjunction — the workhorse of all spacing
analysis — follows formally from the substrate rather than from any new spectral
hypothesis. Why now? Spacing statistics are the most discriminating signature of
random-matrix universality versus Poisson behaviour, and formalizing the
deterministic quantile duality first removes the main technical obstacle before
any probabilistic spacing limit can even be stated.

## 5. Stieltjes transforms and the analytic gateway to limiting laws

This direction defines the empirical Stieltjes transform
`m_s(z) = (1/n) Σ_i 1 / (s i - z)` for `z` off the real axis, relates it to the
empirical CDF via the deterministic identity `m_s(z) = ∫ dF_s(λ)/(λ - z)`, and
proves its elementary analytic properties (holomorphy off the spectrum, the
Nevanlinna/Herglotz sign condition `Im z · Im m_s(z) > 0`, and continuity under the
coordinatewise perturbations controlled by our shift lemmas). The key insight is
that the Stieltjes transform is the *linear functional* dual to the empirical CDF,
so perturbation stability of the CDF transfers directly to stability of the
transform, which is exactly the quantity whose fixed-point equation (e.g.
Marchenko–Pastur) characterizes universal limiting laws. Why now? The Stieltjes
transform is the standard analytic bridge from empirical spectra to named limiting
distributions, and Mathlib's complex-analysis library is now strong enough to
support holomorphy and Herglotz arguments, making this the natural deterministic
precursor to formalizing an actual semicircle- or Marchenko–Pastur-type law.

# A Deterministic Formal Substrate for Empirical Spectral Statistics

## Abstract

Modern studies of large language models (LLMs) repeatedly observe striking
*spectral* regularities: the singular-value spectra of weight matrices, the
eigenvalue spectra of Gram and Hessian matrices, and the empirical distributions
of attention logits all appear to converge, after suitable renormalization, to
universal limiting shapes reminiscent of random-matrix theory. A natural and
ambitious conjecture is that such spectra obey a *universality law*. That
conjecture, taken in full generality, is far too broad to be the statement of a
single Lean theorem: it mixes probabilistic limits, model-specific training
dynamics, and analytic limiting laws.

This module isolates and formalizes the *deterministic, finite-sample core* on
which any such universality argument must rest: the **empirical spectral
cumulative distribution function** (empirical CDF) of a finite real spectrum,
together with its fundamental structural properties. The contribution is a
clean, fully verified Lean 4 / Mathlib foundation — not a claim about any trained
model. All results are proved with no `sorry` and depend only on the standard
axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`.

## 1. The object of study

A *finite real spectrum* of size `n` is a function `s : Fin n → ℝ`. We think of
the values `s 0, …, s (n-1)` as the collected eigenvalues or singular values of
some matrix associated with a model. Its empirical CDF at a threshold `x` is the
fraction of spectral values not exceeding `x`:

```
empiricalCDF s x = (#{ i | s i ≤ x } : ℝ) / (n : ℝ).
```

This is the most basic statistic of a spectrum: it records, for every level `x`,
how much of the spectral mass lies at or below `x`. Histograms, quantiles,
spectral gaps, and spacing distributions are all derived from it, which is why it
is the right primitive to formalize first.

We also formalize a *positive affine renormalization* of a spectrum,
`renormSpectrum a b s = fun i => a * s i + b`, capturing the standard
"center-and-scale" preprocessing (`a > 0`) under which universal limiting shapes
are usually stated.

## 2. Why this is the right deterministic abstraction

Random-matrix universality statements (Wigner semicircle, Marchenko–Pastur,
Tracy–Widom, etc.) are almost always phrased as convergence of *empirical
spectral distributions* — exactly the random measures whose CDFs are the object
above, sampled from a random matrix ensemble. Before one can even state such a
limit, one needs a robust deterministic theory of the empirical CDF as a function
of a *fixed* spectrum:

* it must be a genuine CDF (range in `[0,1]`, monotone in the threshold);
* it must depend only on the multiset of values, not their labelling
  (permutation invariance), because eigenvalues come unordered;
* it must be *stable*: small coordinatewise perturbations of the spectrum move
  the CDF only by a controlled threshold shift (a deterministic Kolmogorov-type
  inequality), which is what lets one pass from approximate to exact spectra;
* it must transform predictably under the center-and-scale renormalization used
  to expose universal shapes.

These are precisely the properties proved here. By separating this deterministic
substrate from the probabilistic layer, later work can add randomness *on top of*
a foundation that is already fully verified, rather than entangling measure
theory with elementary counting facts.

## 3. Formalized results

All statements live in the namespace `EmpiricalSpectrumCDF`
(`MachineLearning/EmpiricalSpectrumCDF.lean`).

### 3.1 Range bounds

* `empiricalCDF_nonneg : 0 ≤ empiricalCDF s x`
* `empiricalCDF_le_one : empiricalCDF s x ≤ 1` (for `[NeZero n]`)

A ratio of a nonnegative count over a nonnegative size is nonnegative; since the
filtered index set is a subset of all `n` indices, the count is at most `n`, so
the ratio is at most `1`.

### 3.2 Threshold monotonicity

* `empiricalCDF_mono : x ≤ y → empiricalCDF s x ≤ empiricalCDF s y`

Raising the threshold can only enlarge the set of indices with `s i ≤ x`, so the
count — and hence the ratio — is monotone. This is the "non-decreasing" half of
being a CDF.

### 3.3 Permutation invariance

* `empiricalCDF_perm : empiricalCDF (fun i => s (e i)) x = empiricalCDF s x`
  for any `e : Fin n ≃ Fin n`.

The empirical CDF depends only on the multiset of spectral values. The proof
rewrites the filtered cardinality as a sum of indicator values and reindexes the
sum along the bijection `e` (`Equiv.sum_comp`). This is essential because the
spectrum of a matrix is intrinsically an unordered collection.

### 3.4 Deterministic perturbation stability (Kolmogorov shift)

* `empiricalCDF_perturb_le :
    (∀ i, |s i - t i| ≤ ε) → empiricalCDF s x ≤ empiricalCDF t (x + ε)`
* `empiricalCDF_perturb_le' :
    (∀ i, |s i - t i| ≤ ε) → empiricalCDF t x ≤ empiricalCDF s (x + ε)`

If two spectra agree coordinatewise up to `ε`, then every index with `s i ≤ x`
satisfies `t i ≤ x + ε`, so the filtered set for `s` at level `x` embeds in the
filtered set for `t` at level `x + ε`. Comparing cardinalities gives the
inequality; the symmetric version follows by exchanging the roles of `s` and `t`
(`abs_sub_comm`). These are deterministic analogues of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov
"horizontal shift" bound and are exactly the tool needed to compare an exact
spectrum to a numerically approximated one.

### 3.5 Affine renormalization compatibility

* `empiricalCDF_renorm :
    0 < a → empiricalCDF (fun i => a * s i + b) x = empiricalCDF s ((x - b) / a)`
* `empiricalCDF_renormSpectrum :
    0 < a → empiricalCDF (renormSpectrum a b s) x = empiricalCDF s ((x - b) / a)`

Under a positive affine change of the spectrum, the CDF is reparametrized by the
inverse change of threshold. The proof reduces the two filter predicates using
the ordered-field equivalence `a * s i + b ≤ x ↔ s i ≤ (x - b) / a`. This is the
algebraic bookkeeping that makes "center-and-scale" preprocessing transparent at
the level of distributions.

## 4. How this supports future universality work

A universality theorem of the informal form "the renormalized empirical spectral
CDF of a random model converges to a fixed limiting profile `F`" decomposes into:

1. a *deterministic* layer describing how the empirical CDF behaves as a function
   of the spectrum — provided here in full;
2. a *probabilistic* layer placing a distribution on spectra (e.g. via a random
   matrix ensemble or an empirical model checkpoint) and proving convergence of
   the random empirical CDF to `F`.

The lemmas above are the standard glue of layer (1): monotonicity and range make
the empirical CDF an honest distribution function; permutation invariance lets
one work with unordered spectra; the perturbation inequalities let one transfer
limits from approximate to exact spectra and bound Kolmogorov–Smirnov distances;
and the renormalization identity is exactly the change of variables used to state
universal limits. With this substrate verified, subsequent formalizations can
focus their effort on the genuinely probabilistic content.

## 5. Scope and honesty of the claims

We deliberately prove **nothing** about any actual trained language model, nor any
probabilistic limit. Every theorem is an elementary, deterministic fact about a
fixed finite function `Fin n → ℝ`. The value of the contribution is precisely
that it is a *clean, reusable, machine-checked foundation* on which more
ambitious empirical and probabilistic spectral-universality claims can later be
built without re-deriving the elementary infrastructure.

# A Finite Infinitesimal Probability Model

This file develops a toy *infinitesimal* probability model on a finite sample
space `Option (Fin n)`.  The sample space consists of `n` "visible" atoms
`some i` together with a single "hidden" atom `none`.

The values of the model do not live in `ℚ` but in the lexicographically ordered
type `LexRat := ℚ ×ₗ ℚ`.  A pair `toLex (a, b)` is to be understood as the
non-standard number `a + b · ε`, where `ε` is a positive infinitesimal smaller
than every positive rational number.  Concretely:

* `ε := toLex (0, 1)` is the infinitesimal,
* the coercion `(r : LexRat)` of a rational `r` is `toLex (r, 0)`,
* `1 = toLex (1, 0)`.

Each visible atom receives weight `ε`, and the hidden atom `none` receives the
weight `1 - n · ε = toLex (1, -n)`, so that the total mass is exactly `1`.

## Main definitions

* `LexRat`            : the value type, `ℚ` ordered lexicographically with an
                        infinitesimal component.
* `LexRat.eps` (`ε`)  : the positive infinitesimal.
* `atomWeight`        : the weight of a single atom.
* `prob`              : the probability of a finite event, the `Finset.sum` of
                        the atom weights.

## Main results

* `eps_pos`, `eps_infinitesimal`      : `ε` is a positive infinitesimal.
* `atomWeight_nonneg`, `prob_nonneg`  : weights and probabilities are nonneg.
* `prob_empty`, `prob_singleton_visible`, `prob_union_disjoint`, `prob_univ`
                                      : basic probability axioms.
* `visible_singleton_infinitesimal`   : a single visible atom has infinitesimal
                                        probability, in particular `< 1`.
-/

open Finset

/-- The value type of the model: rationals with an infinitesimal second
component, ordered lexicographically.  An element `toLex (a, b)` represents the
non-standard number `a + b · ε`. -/
def LexRat : Type := ℚ ×ₗ ℚ

namespace LexRat

instance : LinearOrder LexRat := inferInstanceAs (LinearOrder (ℚ ×ₗ ℚ))
instance : AddCommGroup LexRat := inferInstanceAs (AddCommGroup (ℚ ×ₗ ℚ))
instance : AddLeftMono LexRat := inferInstanceAs (AddLeftMono (ℚ ×ₗ ℚ))
instance : IsOrderedAddMonoid LexRat := inferInstanceAs (IsOrderedAddMonoid (ℚ ×ₗ ℚ))

/-- Build an element of `LexRat` from its standard part `a` and its
infinitesimal coefficient `b`, i.e. the number `a + b · ε`. -/
def mk (a b : ℚ) : LexRat := (toLex (a, b) : ℚ ×ₗ ℚ)

/-- The multiplicative unit `1 = toLex (1, 0)`. -/
instance : One LexRat := ⟨mk 1 0⟩

/-- A rational `r` is embedded as the purely standard number `toLex (r, 0)`. -/
instance : Coe ℚ LexRat := ⟨fun r => mk r 0⟩

@[simp] theorem one_eq : (1 : LexRat) = mk 1 0 := rfl

@[simp] theorem coe_eq (r : ℚ) : (r : LexRat) = mk r 0 := rfl

@[simp] theorem zero_eq : (0 : LexRat) = mk 0 0 := rfl

/-- Addition is componentwise: it adds standard parts and infinitesimal parts
separately. -/
@[simp] theorem mk_add_mk (a b c d : ℚ) : mk a b + mk c d = mk (a + c) (b + d) := rfl

theorem mk_lt_mk {a b c d : ℚ} : mk a b < mk c d ↔ a < c ∨ a = c ∧ b < d :=

theorem mk_le_mk {a b c d : ℚ} : mk a b ≤ mk c d ↔ a < c ∨ a = c ∧ b ≤ d :=

theorem nsmul_mk (n : ℕ) (a b : ℚ) : n • mk a b = mk (n • a) (n • b) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [succ_nsmul, ih, succ_nsmul, succ_nsmul]; rfl

/-- The positive infinitesimal `ε = toLex (0, 1)`. -/
def eps : LexRat := mk 0 1

@[inherit_doc] scoped notation "ε" => LexRat.eps

/-- The infinitesimal is positive. -/
theorem eps_pos : (0 : LexRat) < ε := by
  rw [zero_eq, eps, mk_lt_mk]
  right
  exact ⟨rfl, by norm_num⟩

theorem eps_infinitesimal (r : ℚ) (hr : 0 < r) : ε < (r : LexRat) := by
  rw [coe_eq, eps, mk_lt_mk]
  exact Or.inl hr

/-- The infinitesimal is strictly less than `1`. -/
theorem eps_lt_one : ε < (1 : LexRat) := by
  rw [one_eq, eps, mk_lt_mk]
  exact Or.inl (by norm_num)

end LexRat

open LexRat

section Model

variable (n : ℕ)

/-- The weight assigned to an atom of the sample space `Option (Fin n)`.
Every visible atom `some i` has the infinitesimal weight `ε`, while the hidden
atom `none` carries the remaining mass `1 - n · ε = toLex (1, -n)`. -/
def atomWeight : Option (Fin n) → LexRat
  | none => mk 1 (-(n : ℚ))
  | some _ => ε

@[simp] theorem atomWeight_none : atomWeight n none = mk 1 (-(n : ℚ)) := rfl

@[simp] theorem atomWeight_some (i : Fin n) : atomWeight n (some i) = ε := rfl

/-- Each atom has a nonnegative weight. -/
theorem atomWeight_nonneg : ∀ a, (0 : LexRat) ≤ atomWeight n a
  | none => by
      rw [atomWeight_none, zero_eq, mk_le_mk]
      exact Or.inl (by norm_num)
  | some i => by
      rw [atomWeight_some, eps, zero_eq, mk_le_mk]
      exact Or.inr ⟨rfl, by norm_num⟩

/-- The probability of a finite event `A` is the sum of the weights of its
atoms. -/
def prob (A : Finset (Option (Fin n))) : LexRat := ∑ a ∈ A, atomWeight n a

/-- Probabilities are nonnegative. -/
theorem prob_nonneg (A : Finset (Option (Fin n))) : (0 : LexRat) ≤ prob n A := by
  unfold prob
  exact Finset.sum_nonneg (fun a _ => atomWeight_nonneg n a)

/-- The impossible event has probability `0`. -/
theorem prob_empty : prob n ∅ = 0 := by
  simp [prob]

/-- A single visible atom has probability `ε`. -/
theorem prob_singleton_visible (i : Fin n) :
    prob n ({some i} : Finset (Option (Fin n))) = ε := by
  simp [prob]

/-- Probability is additive over disjoint events. -/
theorem prob_union_disjoint (A B : Finset (Option (Fin n))) (h : Disjoint A B) :
    prob n (A ∪ B) = prob n A + prob n B := by
  unfold prob
  exact Finset.sum_union h

/-- The total probability of the whole sample space is `1`. -/
theorem prob_univ : prob n (Finset.univ : Finset (Option (Fin n))) = 1 := by
  unfold prob
  rw [Fintype.sum_option]
  rw [atomWeight_none]
  have hsum : ∑ i : Fin n, atomWeight n (some i) = mk 0 (n : ℚ) := by
    simp only [atomWeight_some]
    rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin, eps, nsmul_mk]
    simp
  rw [hsum, mk_add_mk, one_eq]
  congr 1 <;> ring

/-- A single visible atom has infinitesimal probability, in particular it is
strictly less than `1`. -/
theorem visible_singleton_infinitesimal (i : Fin n) :
    prob n ({some i} : Finset (Option (Fin n))) < (1 : LexRat) := by
  rw [prob_singleton_visible]
  exact eps_lt_one

end Model

| element            | table (exponent : coeff)      | leading term | sign |
|--------------------|-------------------------------|--------------|------|
| `eps`              | `1 : 1`                       | `+1` at exp 1| `> 0`|
| `q - eps`  (q>0)   | `0 : q`, `1 : -1`             | `+q` at exp 0| `> 0` ⇒ `eps < q` |
| `1 - n·eps`        | `0 : 1`, `1 : -n`             | `+1` at exp 0| `> 0` ⇒ `n·eps < 1` |

* `eps < 1/2, 1/10, 1/1000, …` — yes, since the order-0 coefficient of `q - eps` is

-/

# A Non-Abelianity Certificate for Jones Braid Operators

## Abstract

We formalize, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, the precise algebraic mechanism that makes
Fibonacci / Jones braiding *non-abelian*. Working over an arbitrary field `K`
and an arbitrary (possibly noncommutative) `K`-algebra `A`, we study the Jones
operator attached to a Temperley–Lieb-type generator `X` and a unit `u : Kˣ`,

```
jonesOp u X = (u : K) • 1 + (↑u⁻¹ : K) • X.
```

Our two main results are an exact commutator identity and a sharp
*non-abelianity equivalence*: the Jones images of two generators commute if and
only if the generators themselves commute. This is deliberately **not** a
density or universality statement; it is the clean, fully verified algebraic core
on which such statements (in concrete representations) ultimately rest.

The contribution lives in
`Catalog/Physics/JonesBraidNonabelianCertificate.lean` and reuses the existing
catalog file `Catalog/Algebra/JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.lean`.

## 1. Problem and motivation

Topological quantum computation encodes logical information in the braiding of
anyons. In the Fibonacci / Jones setting, the computational gates are the images
of the braid generators `σ_i` under a representation built from the
Temperley–Lieb algebra. A representation can only be computationally interesting
if it is **non-abelian**: if all braid images commuted, every circuit would
collapse to a diagonal (classical) action and no entangling gate could exist.

The usual story emphasizes the hard analytic fact that, for special parameter
values, the braid images are *dense* in a unitary group `SU(d)` (the
Freedman–Larsen–Wang universality theorem). That density result is genuinely
deep. But underneath it lies a far more elementary and completely general fact:
the Jones map does not *create* or *destroy* commutativity — it transports it
exactly. Two braid images commute precisely when the underlying Temperley–Lieb
generators do. Isolating and certifying this fact is the goal of this note.

## 2. Definitions

Fix a field `K`, a ring `A`, and a `K`-algebra structure `[Algebra K A]`. The
algebra `A` is allowed to be noncommutative (e.g. a matrix algebra).

* **Jones operator (this file).** For a unit `u : Kˣ` and `X : A`,
  ```
  jonesOp u X = (↑u : K) • 1 + (↑u⁻¹ : K) • X.
  ```
  Parametrizing by a *unit* `u` rather than a raw field element makes the
  invertibility of the relevant scalar (`↑u⁻¹`) structural rather than a
  side hypothesis.

* **Catalog Jones operator.** The existing catalog file defines, for a field
  element `A : K`,
  ```
  JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp A X = A • 1 + A⁻¹ • X.
  ```
  We connect the two via `jonesOp_eq_catalog` below; for a unit `u`,
  `jonesOp u X = JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp (↑u) X`.

## 3. Theorem statements

All statements are proved in full (no `sorry`, only the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`).

* **Scalar cancellation** (`unit_smul_eq_zero_iff`).
  For a unit `v : Kˣ` and `z : A`,
  ```
  (↑v : K) • z = 0  ↔  z = 0.
  ```

* **Exact commutator identity** (`jonesOp_commutator`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X * jonesOp u Y - jonesOp u Y * jonesOp u X
    = ((↑u⁻¹ : K) * (↑u⁻¹ : K)) • (X * Y - Y * X).
  ```

* **Non-abelianity equivalence** (`jonesOp_commute_iff`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X * jonesOp u Y = jonesOp u Y * jonesOp u X  ↔  X * Y = Y * X.
  ```

* **Specialization bridge** (`jonesOp_eq_catalog`).
  ```
  jonesOp u X = JonesTemperleyLiebBraid4.jonesOp (↑u : K) X.
  ```

* **Catalog corollary** (`catalog_jonesOp_commute_iff`).
  The same equivalence stated directly for the catalog operator.

* **Concrete example** (`exampleX_mul_exampleY_ne`,
  `example_jonesOp_noncommute`).
  With `X = !![0,1;0,0]` and `Y = !![0,0;1,0]` over `ℚ` we have `XY ≠ YX`, hence
  for *every* rational unit `u` the operators `jonesOp u X` and `jonesOp u Y` do
  not commute.

## 4. Proof sketches

**Scalar cancellation.** If `(↑v) • z = 0`, apply `(↑v⁻¹) •` to both sides; by
`smul_smul` the left side becomes `(↑v⁻¹ * ↑v) • z = (↑(v⁻¹ * v)) • z = 1 • z =
z` while the right side stays `0`. The converse is `smul_zero`.

**Commutator identity.** Unfold `jonesOp` and expand both products with
`mul_add`, `add_mul`, and `smul_smul`. The `1 • 1`, `X`, and `Y` terms are
identical in both orders (scalars in `K` commute), so they cancel under
subtraction. What remains is `(↑u⁻¹)² • (X*Y) - (↑u⁻¹)² • (Y*X)`, which equals
`(↑u⁻¹ * ↑u⁻¹) • (X*Y - Y*X)` by `smul_sub`. The bookkeeping of additive terms is
discharged by `abel`.

**Non-abelianity equivalence.** Rewrite `P = Q` as `P - Q = 0` (`sub_eq_zero`),
substitute the commutator identity, and observe `↑u⁻¹ * ↑u⁻¹ = ↑(u⁻¹ * u⁻¹)`
(`Units.val_mul`). Apply `unit_smul_eq_zero_iff` for the unit `u⁻¹ * u⁻¹` to drop
the nonzero scalar, leaving `X*Y - Y*X = 0`, i.e. `X*Y = Y*X`. This is exactly
the "injectivity of scalar multiplication by the nonzero scalar `(↑u⁻¹)²`"
mentioned in the problem statement.

**Bridge and corollary.** `jonesOp_eq_catalog` is `simp` after unfolding both
definitions, using `↑u⁻¹ = (↑u)⁻¹` in a field. The catalog corollary rewrites the
catalog operator back to `jonesOp u` and invokes the equivalence.

**Concrete example.** The matrix product inequality is settled by evaluating the
`(0,0)` entries (`1` vs `0`). The Jones conclusion is then *immediate* from the
equivalence — no further matrix computation is required, which is precisely the
point of having a bridge theorem.

## 5. Significance for topological quantum compiling

A compiler for a braiding-based architecture must reason about *when* two gates
commute (for scheduling, parallelization, and circuit identities) and must
certify that the gate set is genuinely non-classical. The equivalence
`jonesOp_commute_iff` provides both at the source level:

* commutation of Jones gates is *decidable from* commutation of the much simpler
  Temperley–Lieb generators, so commutation analysis can be pushed down to the
  generator algebra;
* a single non-commuting pair of generators certifies, with no further work,
  that the braid representation is non-abelian — the necessary precondition for
  any entangling gate.

Because the result holds over an arbitrary field and an arbitrary algebra, it
applies uniformly to every concrete model (matrix representations, fusion
categories realized as algebras, parameter specializations), and the verified
`ℚ`-matrix example shows the inference is effective.

## 6. Limitation: this is not a density theorem

We make this explicit. The results here say *nothing* about:

* density of braid images in `SU(d)` or any other group;
* universality for quantum computation;
* topology, anyons, or modular tensor categories beyond their algebraic shadow;
* the special parameter values (roots of unity) at which Fibonacci anyons live.

In particular, non-abelianity is *necessary* but not *sufficient* for
universality. The deep Freedman–Larsen–Wang density theorem is out of scope. What
we contribute is the rigorous, fully general algebraic bridge — *noncommuting
Temperley–Lieb generators give noncommuting Jones braid images, and conversely* —
on top of which density statements for specific representations can later be
built.

open Finset Matrix

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-- **Degenerate spectrum fixes the eigenvector**: a tropical eigenpair with
eigenvalue `0` makes `v` a fixed point of every tropical power of `A`. -/
theorem eigenzero_fixes
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A 0 v) (k : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A k) v i = v i := by
  have := tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A 0 v h k i
  simpa using this

/-- **No exponent leak at `λ = 0`**: every tropical power acts identically on the
degenerate eigenvector `v`, so observing `A^{⊗a} ⊗ v` cannot distinguish the
exponent `a` from any other `b`. This is exactly the failure mode that `tdlp_break`
excludes via its `lam ≠ 0` hypothesis. -/
theorem eigenzero_no_leak
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A 0 v) (a b : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A a) v i = tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A b) v i := by
  rw [eigenzero_fixes A v h a i, eigenzero_fixes A v h b i]

/-- **Concrete witness** that the degenerate regime is non-vacuous: the all-zeros
tropical matrix has tropical eigenvalue `0` on every constant vector. (The min-plus
product with the zero matrix sends a constant vector to itself.) -/
theorem zero_matrix_eigenzero (c : ℝ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (0 : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) 0 (fun _ => c) := by
  intro i
  unfold tropMatVecMul
  simp

/-- **Monotone recovery in the positive regime**: when `λ > 0`, the eigenvalue
`(k+1)λ` of `A^{⊗k}` on `v` is strictly increasing in the exponent `k`. Hence even
without exact division the discrete log is recoverable by monotone (binary) search —
a second, independent attack route. -/

    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (hlam : 0 < lam) (i : Fin n)
    {a b : ℕ} (hab : a < b) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A a) v i < tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A b) v i := by
  rw [tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h a i, tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h b i]

# Tropical Cryptography: Eigenvalue Cryptanalysis of the Tropical Discrete Log

This file formalizes the core mathematics behind the **Tropical Discrete Logarithm
Problem (TDLP)** and the proposed tropical Diffie–Hellman key exchange, building on
the min-plus matrix algebra in `Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra`.

## The scheme (informal)

Over the min-plus semiring `(ℝ, min, +)` one defines the tropical matrix power
`A^{⊗k}` by iterated `tropMatMul`. The proposed key exchange is:

* public `A`, Alice's secret `a`, Bob's secret `b`;
* Alice publishes `A^{⊗a}`, Bob publishes `A^{⊗b}`;
* shared key `A^{⊗ab}` recovered as `(A^{⊗b})^{⊗a} = (A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}`.

The **security conjecture** is that recovering `k` from `(A, A^{⊗k})` (the TDLP) is
hard.

## What we prove

The headline result is a *cryptanalytic* one: the TDLP is **not** hard whenever `A`
has a nonzero tropical eigenvalue. Concretely:

* `tropEigen_pow` — **eigenvalue additivity**: if `(λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair
  of `A`, then `((k+1)λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A^{⊗k}`.
* `tdlp_break` — from the eigenvalue of `A^{⊗k}` on `v` the exponent `k` is uniquely
  determined when `λ ≠ 0`; hence the discrete log leaks.
* `tdlp_recover_formula` — the explicit recovery formula `k + 1 = μ / λ`.
* `tropDH_correct` — the key exchange is *correct*: the shared key is well defined,
  `(A^{⊗a})^{⊗b} = (A^{⊗b})^{⊗a}`.

These together say: the tropical DH protocol runs correctly, but its secret exponents
are recoverable by a single eigenvalue computation, refuting the security conjecture
for the eigenvalue-nondegenerate case.

This file reuses `tropMatMul`, `tropMatVecMul`, `IsTropicalEigenpair`,
`tropMatVecMul_shift`, and `tropMatMul_assoc` from `Tropical.MinPlusAlgebra`.

## References
* Grigoriev, D., Shpilrain, V. "Tropical cryptography" (2014).
* Kotov, M., Ushakov, A. "Analysis of a key exchange protocol based on tropical
  matrix algebra" (2018).
-/

open Finset Matrix

variable {n : ℕ} [NeZero n]

/-! ## Section 1: Tropical matrix power

We index by exponent-minus-one: `tropMatPow A k` denotes `A^{⊗(k+1)}`, the
`(k+1)`-fold tropical product of `A` with itself. This avoids needing a tropical
identity element (which over `ℝ` requires an unbounded "infinity" entry). -/

/-- `tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}`, the `(k+1)`-fold tropical (min-plus) power. -/
def tropMatPow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) : ℕ → Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ
  | 0 => A
  | (k + 1) => tropMatMul A (tropMatPow A k)

@[simp] theorem tropMatPow_zero (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) :
    tropMatPow A 0 = A := rfl

theorem tropMatPow_succ (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (k : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow A (k + 1) = tropMatMul A (tropMatPow A k) := rfl

/-! ## Section 2: Compatibility of matrix and matrix-vector products -/

/-
**Matrix–vector associativity**: `(A ⊗ B) ⊗ v = A ⊗ (B ⊗ v)`. The tropical
matrix-vector action is an action of the multiplicative semigroup of tropical
matrices.
-/
theorem tropMatVecMul_tropMatMul
    (A B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatMul A B) v = tropMatVecMul A (tropMatVecMul B v) := by
  ext i;
  refine' le_antisymm _ _ <;> simp +decide [ tropMatVecMul, tropMatMul ];
  · intro j; obtain ⟨ k, hk ⟩ := Finset.exists_min_image Finset.univ ( fun k => B j k + v k ) ⟨ j, Finset.mem_univ j ⟩ ; use k;
    simp_all +decide [ Finset.inf'_le, Finset.le_inf' ];
    rw [ show ( Finset.univ.inf' Finset.univ_nonempty fun k => B j k + v k ) = B j k + v k from le_antisymm ( Finset.inf'_le _ <| Finset.mem_univ _ ) <| Finset.le_inf' _ _ fun x hx => hk x ] ; linarith [ Finset.inf'_le ( fun k_1 => A i k_1 + B k_1 k ) ( Finset.mem_univ j ) ];
  · intro b; have := Finset.exists_min_image Finset.univ ( fun k => A i k + B k b ) ⟨ b, Finset.mem_univ b ⟩ ; obtain ⟨ k, hk₁, hk₂ ⟩ := this; use k; simp_all +decide [ Finset.inf'_eq_csInf_image ] ;
    rw [ ← sub_le_iff_le_add ];
    refine' le_csInf _ _ <;> norm_num;
    · exact ⟨ _, ⟨ k, rfl ⟩ ⟩;
    · intro a; linarith [ hk₂ a, show sInf ( Set.range fun k_1 => B k k_1 + v k_1 ) ≤ B k b + v b from csInf_le ( Set.finite_range _ |> Set.Finite.bddBelow ) ( Set.mem_range_self _ ) ] ;

/-! ## Section 3: Power laws (semigroup structure) -/

/-
**Power product law**: `A^{⊗(a+1)} ⊗ A^{⊗(b+1)} = A^{⊗(a+b+2)}`.
-/
theorem tropMatMul_pow_pow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatMul (tropMatPow A a) (tropMatPow A b) = tropMatPow A (a + b + 1) := by
  induction' a with a ih generalizing b;
  · grind +locals;
  · grind +suggestions

/-
**Power of a power**: `(A^{⊗(a+1)})^{⊗(b+1)} = A^{⊗((a+1)(b+1))}`.
-/
theorem tropMatPow_tropMatPow (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b = tropMatPow A ((a + 1) * (b + 1) - 1) := by
  induction' b with b ih;
  · aesop;
  · convert tropMatMul_pow_pow A ( a ) ( ( a + 1 ) * ( b + 1 ) - 1 ) using 1;
    · rw [ ← ih, tropMatPow_succ ];
    · exact congr_arg _ ( Nat.sub_eq_of_eq_add <| by linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel ( by nlinarith : 1 ≤ ( a + 1 ) * ( b + 1 ) ) ] )

/-! ## Section 4: Tropical Diffie–Hellman correctness -/

/-
**Tropical DH correctness**: the shared key is well defined — Alice computing
`(A^{⊗b})^{⊗a}` and Bob computing `(A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}` obtain the same matrix.
-/
theorem tropDH_correct (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (a b : ℕ) :
    tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b = tropMatPow (tropMatPow A b) a := by
  rw [ tropMatPow_tropMatPow, tropMatPow_tropMatPow ];
  rw [ Nat.mul_comm ]

/-! ## Section 5: Eigenvalue additivity and the TDLP break -/

/-
The matrix-vector action of a power on an eigenvector scales by the exponent:
`A^{⊗(k+1)} ⊗ v = v + (k+1)λ`. This is `tropEigen_pow` in eigenpair language.
-/
theorem tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) (i : Fin n) :
    tropMatVecMul (tropMatPow A k) v i = v i + (k + 1) * lam := by
  induction' k with k ih generalizing i;
  · simpa using h i;
  · convert
      ( show tropMatVecMul ( tropMatMul A ( tropMatPow A k ) ) v i =
          tropMatVecMul A ( fun j => v j + ( k + 1 ) * lam ) i from ?_ ) using 1;
    · have := tropMatVecMul_shift A v ( ( k + 1 ) * lam ) i;
      rw [ this, h i ] ; push_cast ; ring;
    · rw [ tropMatVecMul_tropMatMul ];
      exact congr_arg ( fun f => tropMatVecMul A f i ) ( funext ih )

/-
**Eigenvalue additivity**: if `(λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A`, then
`((k+1)λ, v)` is a tropical eigenpair of `A^{⊗(k+1)} = tropMatPow A k`.

This is the structural fact that makes the tropical discrete log easy: eigenvalues
are additive under powering.
-/
theorem tropEigen_pow
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (k : ℕ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A k) ((k + 1) * lam) v := by
  intro i; rw [ show ( ( k : ℝ ) + 1 ) * lam = ( k + 1 ) * lam by ring ] ; exact mod_cast tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h k i;

/-
**TDLP break (uniqueness)**: if `A` has a nonzero tropical eigenvalue `λ` on
`v`, then any two powers of `A` that act on `v` by the same scalar `μ` must have the
same exponent. Hence the secret exponent in the tropical DH scheme is uniquely
determined by the eigenvalue of the published matrix — the discrete log leaks.
-/
theorem tdlp_break
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (hlam : lam ≠ 0) (mu : ℝ) (a b : ℕ)
    (ha : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A a) mu v)
    (hb : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A b) mu v) :
    a = b := by
  -- From the eigenvalue equations, we have that $mu = (a + 1) * lam$ and $mu = (b + 1) * lam$.
  have hmu_a : mu = (a + 1) * lam := by
    have := tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h a;
    linarith [ ha ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩, this ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ]
  have hmu_b : mu = (b + 1) * lam := by
    have := hb ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ; have := @tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen n _ A lam v h b ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ; aesop;
  exact_mod_cast ( mul_right_cancel₀ hlam <| by linarith : ( a : ℝ ) = b )

/-
**Explicit recovery formula**: from the public matrix `B = A^{⊗(k+1)}` one reads
off its eigenvalue `μ = (k+1)λ` on the shared eigenvector `v`, and recovers the
secret exponent via `k + 1 = μ / λ`.
-/
theorem tdlp_recover_formula
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (hlam : lam ≠ 0) (k : ℕ) (mu : ℝ)
    (hmu : IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow A k) mu v) :
    (k : ℝ) + 1 = mu / lam := by
  rw [ eq_div_iff hlam, mul_comm ];
  linarith [ hmu ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩, tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen A lam v h k ⟨ 0, NeZero.pos n ⟩ ]

/-
The shared DH key acts on the common eigenvector by the *product* of the secret
exponents (plus the offsets): `((A^{⊗a})^{⊗b}) ⊗ v = v + ((a+1)(b+1)) λ`.
-/
theorem tropDH_shared_eigen
    (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℝ) (lam : ℝ) (v : Fin n → ℝ)
    (h : IsTropicalEigenpair A lam v) (a b : ℕ) :
    IsTropicalEigenpair (tropMatPow (tropMatPow A a) b) (((a + 1) * (b + 1) : ℕ) * lam) v := by
  convert tropEigen_pow ( tropMatPow A a ) ( ( a + 1 ) * lam ) v ( tropEigen_pow A lam v h a ) b using 1 ; push_cast ; ring

end

The objects live in the min-plus semiring `(ℝ, min, +)`; the matrix powers use

## 1. A 2×2 worked example of eigenvalue additivity

Let
```
A = [ 0   3 ]
    [ 2   0 ]   (min-plus)
```
Take the candidate eigenvector `v = (0, 0)` and `λ = 0`? Check:
`(A ⊗ v)_1 = min(0+0, 3+0) = 0`, `(A ⊗ v)_2 = min(2+0, 0+0) = 0`. So `(0, v)` is an
eigenpair — a *degenerate* spectrum, matching `zero_matrix_eigenzero`-style behaviour:
every power fixes `v`, no exponent leaks (cf. `eigenzero_no_leak`).

Now a **nondegenerate** example. Let
```
A = [ 5   3 ]
    [ 3   5 ]
```
with `v = (0,0)`. Then `(A ⊗ v)_i = min(5, 3) = 3`, so `(3, v)` is an eigenpair, `λ = 3`.

Tropical square `A^{⊗2} = A ⊗ A`:
`(A²)_{11} = min(5+5, 3+3) = 6`, `(A²)_{12} = min(5+3, 3+5) = 8`, symmetric.
```
A^{⊗2} = [ 6  8 ]
         [ 8  6 ]
```
`(A² ⊗ v)_i = min(6, 8) = 6 = 0 + 2·3`. Eigenvalue **doubled**: `λ(A^{⊗2}) = 6 = 2λ(A)`.

`A^{⊗3}`: `(A³)_{11} = min(6+5, 8+3) = 11`, so `(A³ ⊗ v)_i = min(11, 13) = 11`? Recompute
the off-diagonal: `(A³)_{12} = min(6+3, 8+5) = 9`, so `(A³ ⊗ v)_i = min(11, 9) = 9 = 3·3`.
Eigenvalue **tripled**: `λ(A^{⊗3}) = 9 = 3λ(A)`. ✓

This is exactly `tropMatVecMul_pow_eigen`: `λ(A^{⊗k}) = (k+1)λ` (index offset: our
`tropMatPow A k = A^{⊗(k+1)}`).

## 2. TDLP recovery check

Given the public `A` above (`λ = 3`) and a published `B = A^{⊗k}` with measured
eigenvalue `μ`:

| k (exponent) | μ = (k)·λ | recovered k = μ/λ |
|--------------|-----------|-------------------|
| 1            | 3         | 1                 |
| 2            | 6         | 2                 |
| 3            | 9         | 3                 |
| 10           | 30        | 10                |

Recovery is a single division — the formal content of `tdlp_recover_formula`. The
exponent is **never** hidden when `λ ≠ 0`, refuting the TDLP-hardness conjecture for
nondegenerate spectra.

## 3. Diffie–Hellman correctness check

Shared key exponent for secrets `a`, `b` (with our offset) is `(a+1)(b+1)`, symmetric
in `a, b`. E.g. `a=2, b=3 → 12`; `a=3, b=2 → 12`. Both parties land on `A^{⊗12}`,
confirming `tropDH_correct`.

- Hunt for a nondegenerate (`λ ≠ 0`) instance where the eigenvalue is **not** additive
  under powering: none found; additivity is forced by `tropMatVecMul_shift` +
  associativity (now proved).
- Hunt for a `λ ≠ 0` instance where two distinct exponents share an eigenvalue on the
  same `v`: impossible, since `k ↦ (k+1)λ` is injective (`tdlp_break`).
- The **only** indistinguishability arises at `λ = 0` (`eigenzero_no_leak`), found
  immediately via the all-zeros / constant-diagonal matrices.

The shared-key exponent table `(a+1)(b+1)` is just the multiplication table (no novel
integer sequence); no OEIS lookup is warranted. The eigenvalue sequence `k ↦ kλ` is a
trivial arithmetic progression. The interesting content is structural, not numeric,
which is why the formal proofs (not the numerics) are the deliverable.

/-!
# Anti-Gravity Mathematics: structural laws of dependency DAGs

We model a formal library as a finite **dependency DAG**: vertices are theorems
and `dep a b` means "theorem `a` (transitively) depends on theorem `b`", so `b`
is the more fundamental theorem.  Because we model *transitive reachability* of an
acyclic graph, `dep` is a strict partial order (transitive + irreflexive).

The **gravitational weight** of a theorem `b` is the number of theorems that
depend on it.  A theorem is **anti-gravity** when its weight is large but its
proof cost is small.  This file proves the structural laws that survive scrutiny;
`Examples.lean` constructs the libraries that refute the over-strong "10% law".

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis (Hypothesizer): the right invariant of a library is the weight
function `weight b = #{a : dep a b}`, and the basic conservation/monotonicity
laws of dependency DAGs are theorems, not heuristics.

Experiment (Experimenter): formalize `DepDAG`, `weight`, and `IsAntiGravity`;
prove (1) strict monotonicity of weight along dependency, (2) the conservation
law relating total weight to the number of dependency pairs, and (3) existence of
an at-least-average ("foundational") theorem.

Analysis (Analyst): all three survive. Monotonicity is the engine: it is the
formal content of "deeper theorems carry more weight". Conservation is an exact
double count, not an inequality. The average bound is what makes "some theorem is
heavy" unconditional.

Critique (Critic): none of these is vacuous — monotonicity needs a genuine strict
`Finset.card_lt_card`, conservation a genuine double count, and the average bound a
genuine extremal argument. See `Examples.lean` for the adversarial counterexample
to the conjectured density/10% claim.

namespace AntiGravity

open Finset

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V]

/-- A dependency DAG on a (finite) set of theorems.  `dep a b` reads
"theorem `a` depends on theorem `b`"; `b` is the more fundamental theorem.
We model transitive reachability, hence a strict partial order. -/
structure DepDAG (V : Type*) where
  /-- `dep a b`: theorem `a` depends on theorem `b`. -/
  dep : V → V → Prop
  /-- Dependency is transitive (reachability composes). -/
  trans' : ∀ ⦃a b c⦄, dep a b → dep b c → dep a c
  /-- Nothing depends on itself (acyclicity). -/
  irrefl' : ∀ a, ¬ dep a a

open Classical in
/-- The finset of theorems that depend on `b`. -/
noncomputable def DepDAG.dependents (G : DepDAG V) (b : V) : Finset V :=
  univ.filter (fun a => G.dep a b)

/-- The **gravitational weight** of `b`: how many theorems depend on it. -/
noncomputable def DepDAG.weight (G : DepDAG V) (b : V) : ℕ := (G.dependents b).card

@[simp] lemma DepDAG.mem_dependents (G : DepDAG V) {a b : V} :
    a ∈ G.dependents b ↔ G.dep a b := by
  classical
  simp [DepDAG.dependents]

/-- **Gravitational monotonicity.** If `a` depends on `b`, then `b` is strictly
heavier than `a`: every dependent of `a` is a dependent of `b` (transitivity), and
`a` itself depends on `b` but not on itself. -/
theorem DepDAG.weight_lt_of_dep (G : DepDAG V) {u t : V} (h : G.dep u t) :
    G.weight u < G.weight t := by
  refine' Finset.card_lt_card _;
  simp_all +decide [ Finset.ssubset_def, Finset.subset_iff ];
  exact ⟨ fun x hx => G.trans' hx h, u, h, G.irrefl' u ⟩

open Classical in
/-- **Conservation law.** The total gravitational weight of the library equals the
number of dependency pairs. -/
theorem DepDAG.sum_weight_eq (G : DepDAG V) :
    ∑ b, G.weight b
      = (univ.filter (fun p : V × V => G.dep p.1 p.2)).card := by
  unfold DepDAG.weight
  simp +decide only [dependents, card_filter]
  exact Eq.symm (Fintype.sum_prod_type_right fun x => if G.dep x.1 x.2 then 1 else 0)

/-- There is always a maximally-heavy ("most foundational") theorem. -/
theorem DepDAG.exists_max_weight (G : DepDAG V) [Nonempty V] :
    ∃ b : V, ∀ a : V, G.weight a ≤ G.weight b := by
  simpa using Finset.exists_max_image Finset.univ ( fun a => G.weight a ) ( Finset.univ_nonempty )

/-- **Above-average foundation.** Some theorem carries at least the average weight:
its weight times the library size dominates the total weight. -/
theorem DepDAG.exists_weight_ge_average (G : DepDAG V) [Nonempty V] :
    ∃ b : V, (∑ a, G.weight a) ≤ Fintype.card V * G.weight b := by
  obtain ⟨ b, hb ⟩ := DepDAG.exists_max_weight G;
  exact ⟨ b, le_trans ( Finset.sum_le_sum fun _ _ => hb _ ) ( by simp +decide ) ⟩

/-- A theorem `b` is **anti-gravity** for thresholds `(wT, cT)` and cost
function `cost` if its weight is at least `wT` while its proof cost is at most
`cT`: high weight, short proof. -/
def DepDAG.IsAntiGravity (G : DepDAG V) (cost : V → ℕ) (wT cT : ℕ) (b : V) : Prop :=
  wT ≤ G.weight b ∧ cost b ≤ cT

end AntiGravity

open Finset

/-- A genuine three-theorem fragment of the catalog, as a dependency chain
`0 ≺ 1 ≺ 2`: node `0` (the irrationality of `e`) is depended on by both downstream
nodes. `dep a b` means "a depends on b", encoded as `b < a`. -/

  trans' := fun _ _ _ h1 h2 => lt_trans h2 h1
  irrefl' := fun a => lt_irrefl a

/-- The mathematical statement attached to each node of the fragment.  Node `0` is
the foundational irrationality result; the downstream nodes are abstracted to `True`
(their content is irrelevant to the dependency structure). -/

  | 0 => Irrational (Real.exp 1)
  | _ => True

/-- Every node of the fragment is a genuine theorem.  Node `0` is discharged by the
catalog result `exp_nat_irrational`. -/

  intro i
  fin_cases i
  · show Irrational (Real.exp 1)
    simpa using exp_nat_irrational 1 (le_refl 1)
  · exact trivial
  · exact trivial

/-- **The foundational node is strictly the heaviest.**  Using the abstract
gravitational-monotonicity law, the irrationality-of-`e` node strictly outweighs
both downstream nodes that depend on it. -/

    (∀ i : Fin 3, nivenStmt i) ∧
      nivenChain.weight 1 < nivenChain.weight 0 ∧
        nivenChain.weight 2 < nivenChain.weight 0 := by
  refine ⟨nivenStmt_true, ?_, ?_⟩
  · exact nivenChain.weight_lt_of_dep (show (0 : Fin 3) < 1 by decide)
  · exact nivenChain.weight_lt_of_dep (show (0 : Fin 3) < 2 by decide)

  simp +decide [ DepDAG.weight ];
  simp +decide [ DepDAG.dependents ];
  convert Finset.card_filter ( fun a : Fin 3 => 0 < a ) Finset.univ

`2` (everyone depends on it) and proof cost `0` in this fragment: high weight,

theorem niven_foundation_antigravity :
    nivenChain.IsAntiGravity (fun _ => 0) 2 0 0 :=

namespace AntiGravity

open Finset

/-! ## The fan library -/

/-- `fanDAG n`: a single foundational theorem `0` on which all of the other `n+1`
theorems depend, and no other dependencies. -/
def fanDAG (n : ℕ) : DepDAG (Fin (n + 2)) where
  dep a b := b = 0 ∧ a ≠ 0
  trans' := by rintro a b c ⟨hb, _⟩ ⟨_, hb'⟩; exact absurd hb hb'
  irrefl' := by rintro a ⟨ha0, ha⟩; exact ha ha0

/-
In the fan library the foundational theorem `0` has weight `n+1`.
-/
theorem fanDAG_weight_zero (n : ℕ) : (fanDAG n).weight (0 : Fin (n + 2)) = n + 1 := by
  simp +decide [ fanDAG, DepDAG.weight, DepDAG.dependents ];
  simp +decide [ Finset.filter_ne' ]

/-- **Guaranteed anti-gravity theorem.**  The fan library always contains a theorem
of weight `n+1` and proof cost `0`: high weight, short proof. -/
theorem antigravity_exists (n : ℕ) :
    ∃ b : Fin (n + 2), (fanDAG n).IsAntiGravity (fun _ => 0) (n + 1) 0 b :=
  ⟨0, (fanDAG_weight_zero n).ge, le_refl 0⟩

/-! ## The chain library -/

/-- `chainDAG k`: a tower `0 ≺ 1 ≺ ⋯ ≺ k` where `a` depends on `b` iff `b < a`. -/
def chainDAG (k : ℕ) : DepDAG (Fin (k + 1)) where
  dep a b := b < a
  trans' := fun _ _ _ h1 h2 => lt_trans h2 h1
  irrefl' := fun a => lt_irrefl a

/-
A chain theorem has positive weight iff it is not the most recent (top) one.
-/
theorem chain_weight_pos_iff (k : ℕ) (b : Fin (k + 1)) :
    1 ≤ (chainDAG k).weight b ↔ b ≠ Fin.last k := by
  simp +decide [ DepDAG.weight, chainDAG ];
  simp +decide [ DepDAG.dependents, Finset.Nonempty ];
  exact ⟨ fun ⟨ a, ha ⟩ => ne_of_lt ( lt_of_lt_of_le ha ( Fin.le_last _ ) ), fun hb => ⟨ Fin.last _, lt_of_le_of_ne ( Fin.le_last _ ) hb ⟩ ⟩

open Classical in
/-- **Chain density.**  With weight threshold `1` and cost `0`, exactly `k` of the
`k+1` theorems in the chain are anti-gravity — fraction `k/(k+1) → 1`. -/
theorem chain_antigravity_card (k : ℕ) :

  unfold chainDAG; simp +decide [ DepDAG.IsAntiGravity ]
  convert Finset.card_erase_of_mem ( Finset.mem_univ ( Fin.last k ) ) using 2
  · ext; simp +decide [ Finset.mem_erase, Finset.mem_univ ]
    convert chain_weight_pos_iff k _ using 1
  · simp +decide [ Finset.card_univ ]

/-! ## The discrete library and the refutation of the "10% law" -/

/-- `discreteDAG V`: independent facts with no dependencies at all. -/
def discreteDAG (V : Type*) : DepDAG V where
  dep _ _ := False
  trans' := fun _ _ _ h _ => h.elim
  irrefl' := fun _ h => h

/-- Every theorem in the discrete library has weight `0`. -/
theorem discrete_weight (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (b : V) :
    (discreteDAG V).weight b = 0 := by
  unfold DepDAG.weight;
  unfold DepDAG.dependents; aesop;

open Classical in
/-- **The "10% law" is false.**  There is a positive-size library in which *no*
theorem is anti-gravity (the discrete library): its anti-gravity fraction is `0`,
not `10%`. -/
theorem ten_percent_law_false :

  -- Consider the discrete library with 3 elements.

  -- Define the discrete library with 3 elements.
  use inferInstance, discreteDAG (Fin 3), fun _ => 0;
  unfold DepDAG.IsAntiGravity; simp +decide [ discrete_weight ] ;

end AntiGravity

| 2 | 4      | 3         | 0               | 1                                | 1/4      |
| 8 | 10     | 9         | 0               | 1                                | 1/10     |

Vertices `Fin (k+1)`; `dep a b ↔ b < a`. weight(b) = k − b.

| k | #nodes | weights        | #anti-gravity (wT = 1, cost 0) | fraction   |
|---|--------|----------------|--------------------------------|------------|
| 1 | 2      | 1,0            | 1                              | 1/2        |
| 2 | 3      | 2,1,0          | 2                              | 2/3        |
| 9 | 10     | 9,8,...,1,0    | 9                              | 9/10       |

Vertices `Fin m`; `dep a b ↔ False`. Every weight is 0.

| m | #anti-gravity (wT = 1) | fraction |
|---|------------------------|----------|
| 3 | 0                      | 0        |

The mission **predicts "10% of theorems in any formal library are anti-gravity"**

fixed weight threshold:

* `D_m` gives fraction **0%** (no node has any dependent at all).
* `C_k` with threshold 1 gives fraction **k/(k+1) → 100%**.
* `F_n` with threshold n+1 gives fraction **1/(n+2) → 0%**.

* **Above-average foundation**: some theorem has weight ≥ the library average.
* **Guarded existence**: anti-gravity theorems *do* exist in the fan family.

These are what we formalize. The density/10% claim is recorded as refuted and
replaced by guarded existence + an extremal-range statement.
